scenes.heading: Partitioning Fundamentals
scenes.narration: Partitioning splits a large table into smaller pieces by column value, so queries scan only what they need.

scenes.heading: Why partitioning helps
bullets: Loads and deletes can target whole partitions.
The right key is low-cardinality and query-aligned.
scenes.narration: When a query filters on the partition column, the engine prunes away partitions it does not need, scanning far less data. Independent partitions also process in parallel, boosting throughput. Choosing a key that matches common filters and avoids too many tiny files is what makes partitioning pay off.

scenes.heading: Partitioning by date
scenes.narration: Partitioning by event_date physically groups rows by day. The query filters on that same column, so the engine reads only the folder for May first and ignores every other day. This pruning is the whole point, turning a full-table scan into a tiny targeted read.

scenes.heading: Under vs over-partitioning
scenes.narration: If partitions are too large, queries still scan more than they should and lose the pruning benefit. If partitions are too fine, you drown in tiny files whose metadata overhead cripples performance. The art is choosing a granularity that keeps partitions substantial but still prunable.

scenes.text: Partitioning divides data by a well-chosen key so queries prune irrelevant data, but the key's granularity must avoid both giant and tiny partitions.
scenes.narration: Pick a partition key that matches how people actually filter, and keep partition sizes healthy to sidestep the small-file trap.
